power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Educational technologies (EdTech) are increasingly used to support neurodivergent learners in primary classrooms, yet their educational value remains difficult to establish across diverse learners, technologies, and contexts.
We address this challenge through a scoping review of EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms, screening 3,340 records across six research databases and including 93 studies.

The findings reveal an uneven evidence base, concentrated on autistic learners, individualised academic and cognitive support, and emerging technologies such as virtual reality, robotics, and artificial intelligence, while social, communicative, and peer-interaction outcomes received less attention.
Design and evaluation processes were frequently researcher-led or unreported, with limited participation from children and other stakeholders.
Intended goals and evaluated outcomes were often misaligned, and educational value was predominantly validated by researchers rather than by those using the technologies in classrooms.

Building on these findings, we argue that educational value is constructed across three interconnected dimensions: conceptual (what counts as valuable), operational (how value is measured), and endorsed (whose judgements validate it).
When these dimensions are disconnected, claims of educational value can become detached from the priorities and experiences of those the technologies are intended to serve.

In response, we propose two complementary frameworks: one to guide future EdTech research and development, and another to help practitioners assess the educational value and relevance of EdTech for their classrooms.
An estimated 10-20% of the school-age population is neurodivergent (Department of Education, 2026).

text.text: Existing reviews have examined specific technologies, neurodevelopmental conditions, or skill domains, often across K-12 or clinical settings (Section 2.2), limiting their relevance for primary practitioners.

To our knowledge, no previous review has synthesised evidence across technologies and neurodivergent learner profiles specifically for primary classrooms while examining how educational value is defined and evaluated.

The literature therefore remains conceptually, methodologically and empirically fragmented, making it difficult to establish what is known, where evidence converges or diverges, and which questions remain unresolved.
To address these gaps, we conducted a scoping review of EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms.
Rather than evaluating the effectiveness of individual technologies, we examine what counts as success, how it is established, and for whom.

The review has two aims: (1) to map how EdTech is conceptualised, designed, adopted and evaluated in neuro-inclusive primary classrooms across learner profiles and educational contexts, identifying key gaps; and (2) to develop two complementary frameworks, one to guide future research and development and another to help practitioners assess EdTech's relevance and readiness for specific classroom contexts.
Four research questions guide the review: RQ1.
Which neurodivergent learner profiles, educational contexts, technology types and intended goals are represented in the literature on EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms?
RQ2.
How is EdTech designed and developed according to the literature, and to what extent are neurodivergent children and other stakeholders involved?
How is EdTech adopted in primary classroom practice according to the literature?
How are the intended goals of EdTech operationalised and validated, and to what extent are neurodivergent children and other stakeholders reported to be involved in the evaluation?

text.text: Collectively, these reviews affirm EdTech's growing relevance for neurodivergent learners but share three limitations.
First, the evidence base is fragmented, and the literature presents isolated technologies and neurodivergent profiles, described in widely varying terminology, rather than a coherent landscape.
Second, very few reviews focus on primary classrooms; most span K-12 or wider age ranges, or clinical and therapeutic settings, limiting their relevance for primary practitioners.
Third, no review examines how educational value is constructed across the technology lifecycle, from design through adoption to evaluation.
As a result, both the evidence itself and its relevance to adoption decisions remain uncertain, limiting its practical utility for schools.
The present review addresses these limitations.
We conducted a scoping review following (Peters et al., 2015).

The literature search was conducted across six major academic databases: ACM Digital Library, ERIC (Educational Resources Information Center), PsycINFO, IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers), Scopus, and WOS (Web of Science), selected for their complementary coverage of this interdisciplinary topic.
The latest search was conducted on 9 August 2026 for studies written in English published from 2015 onwards.
Eligible studies were required to address all three elements of the

Joanna Briggs Institute's PCC (Population, Concept, Context) scoping review framework (Joanna Briggs Institute, 2015): Population: Neurodivergent primary school children, encompassing a range of developmental conditions and experiences, based on classifications outlined in the (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders: DSM-5, 2013) and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) by (World HealthOrganization (WHO), 2019).
Concept: Educational technologies, in full-text, peer-reviewed journal articles or conference proceedings written in English and published from 2015.
Context: Educational technologies that are designed, adopted, or evaluated for primary school classroom settings, including home-schooling.
Studies of technologies not clearly associated with classroom practice, or of technology broadly (e.g.
ICT), were excluded.
Unpublished data or grey literature, reviews, protocols, and non-English articles were excluded.

text.text: Autism (ASD) was the most studied profile (n=37, 39.8%), followed by intellectual/cognitive disabilities (n=22, 23.7%), ADHD (n=16, 17.2%), and dyslexia (n=15, 16.1%).
A further 14 (15.1%) articles focused on general learning disabilities/difficulties without specifying a particular profile.

Language disorder/delay was represented in only six articles (6.5%), and other profiles, including dysgraphia, Down syndrome, developmental delay, and visual or auditory processing difficulties, appeared in one to three studies each (1.1-3.2%).
Regarding the educational context, most studies took place in mainstream schools (n = 63, 67.7%), followed by Special Educational Needs (SEN) schools (n = 16, 17.2%) and homeschooling (n = 7, 7.5%).
Seven studies (7.5%) did not report a setting.
At classroom level, inclusive classes (n=36, 38.7%) and special classes (n=33, 35.5%) were similarly common.

The most frequent school-classroom combination were inclusive classes in mainstream schools (n = 33, 35.5%), followed by special classes in mainstream schools (n = 20, 21.5%) and special classes in SEN schools (n = 13, 14.0%).
Resource rooms, home settings and mixed special/inclusive classes were rare.
Fifteen studies (16.1%) did not report classroom type (Figure .

Extended reality (XR: VR, AR, MR) was the most studied technology category (n = 26, 28.0%), followed by robotics and embodied technologies (n = 14, 15.1%), AI-driven systems (n = 12, 12.9%) and mobile/tablet applications (n = 10, 10.8%).
Game-based learning and multimedia/content-based tools accounted for nine studies each (9.7%).

The remaining 13 studies spanned five categories, each under 5%: platforms and digital environments, assistive and accessibility technologies, classroom interaction tools, sensor-based systems, and multimodal integrated systems (Figure 4).

text.text: The results reveal substantial technological and methodological diversity but offer limited clarity about what constitutes meaningful educational value in neuro-inclusive educational technologies (EdTech) and how it should be validated.

Here, we discuss the findings through two questions: a) what does the existing evidence show across each research question, including the research gaps and their implications for establishing evidence of educational value and b) what this implies for future research and practice.

From these, we derive two complementary frameworks: one to guide future research and development (Section 5.2.5), and one to support practitioners in appraising EdTech for their classrooms (Section 6).
The evidence base provides an uneven representation of neurodevelopmental profiles, technologies, educational contexts, and intended goals.

Research concentrated on particular learner profiles, especially ASD, and emerging technologies such as VR, robotics, and AI, while other learner profiles and technology types received comparatively less attention.
Studies were similarly concentrated in mainstream and inclusive classrooms, with less evidence from SEN schools and home settings.
Intended goals were predominantly academic and cognitive, with considerably less attention to socio-emotional, communicative, peerinteraction, and affective outcomes.

These goal patterns also varied across learner profiles, with dyslexia and dyscalculia primarily associated with academic goals, while socioemotional goals were most explicitly associated with ASD learners (Section 4.1).
The evidence therefore provides uneven coverage of the diversity of neurodivergent learners, their educational needs, or the range of technologies that could support them.

This pattern may reflect intersecting research priorities and assumptions across educational, technological, clinical and diagnostic domains (Kucirkova et al., 2025), although the underlying reasons for these concentrations cannot be established from the present evidence.

text.text: This interpretation is consistent with earlier reviews that have similarly concentrated around particular populations, technologies, or educational goals.

For example, robotics research on autism has emphasised social-emotional learning (Kewalramani et al., 2024) or technology-enhanced interventions for students with dyslexia (Skočić Mihić et al., 2022).

text.text: Evidence of child-centred design in neuro-inclusive EdTech is limited.
Design processes were frequently unreported or researcher-led, and participatory approaches involving teachers and children remained a minority.
Although children were the primary users in most studies, they were identified as design partners in only one.
Teachers, by contrast, were less often represented as users, yet occupied a broader range of design roles than children.
The resulting technologies were predominantly built around multimodal, individualised interaction, with less attention to social, collaborative, and shared classroom experiences (Section 4.2).
Taken together, the design evidence in this field thus remains opaque and strongly adultdefined.

This may reflect long-standing challenges in designing with children (Druin, 1999; Frauenberger et al., 2015) and the historical exclusion of neurodivergent learners from decisions concerning their educational experiences.

text.text: The emphasis on sensory-rich, individualised technological interactions may likewise represent researchers' and educators' assumptions about what constitutes meaningful technological value for neurodivergent learners, rather than evidence grounded in neurodivergent children's experiences of neuroinclusive classrooms (Schmidt & Glaser, 2026; Spiel et al., 2019).

text.text: Classroom adoption of neuro-inclusive EdTech followed a relatively narrow model.
Individual child-technology interaction dominated, with the whole-class and small-group adoption a small minority.
Teachers mostly facilitated or scaffolded these individual interactions as needed, rarely using the technology themselves or integrating it into wider classroom activity (Section 4.3).
Neuro-inclusive EdTech therefore appears to function mainly as support for individual children within existing classroom practice, rather than as a means of changing collective practice.

One possible explanation, which the review cannot directly establish, is that individualised adoption aligns more readily with conventional classroom models and standardised assessment, particularly where educational success is framed in individual academic terms.

We do not argue that EdTech should necessarily be designed for whole-class use, but question how the current individualised technologies support children's participation in the wider classroom, including opportunities for shared activity, peer interaction, and classroom membership (Bauminger-Zviely et al., 2013; Fage et al., 2019).

text.text: The findings reveal a mismatch between conceptual, operational, and endorsed educational value.
Intended goals did not always correspond to the outcomes evaluated, and some outcomes not stated as intended goals became prominent in evaluation.

The operational educational value may thus diverge from the conceptual one, introducing criteria that serve as indicators of value alongside, or in place of, the goals the technology was intended to achieve.
The same asymmetry extends to the endorsement, that is, whose judgments are treated as legitimate in determining whether educational value has been achieved.

Children took part in most evaluations, but largely as subjects of assessment or as respondents to researcher-defined dimensions; teachers typically responded to researcher-designed questionnaires, and domain experts and parents were mostly absent.
Evaluation therefore remained largely researcher-led, with children and teachers having little influence over what counted as educational value (Section 4.4).
The evidence gap therefore concerns not only the quantity of evidence, but also what is conceptualised as value, how it is operationalised, and who endorses it as educational success.

We interpret this as a potential epistemic limitation, and the evidence offers a narrow account of educational value because the perspectives and priorities shaping its definition and evaluation are themselves unevenly distributed.

The divergence between conceptual and operational value may also reflect wider EdTech decision-making, in which procurement teams and policymakers weigh features such as usability alongside educational impact.

When researchers predominantly authorise evaluation, the resulting evidence may privilege one perspective and provide a more limited account of how value is experienced by those who use the technology in practice.

Our findings therefore extend existing concerns about the limited evidence base for EdTech by showing that the problem is not only a lack of evidence, but a lack of diverse perspectives in producing it (Kucirkova et al., 2025 (Kucirkova et al., , 2026;; Lai et al., 2022).

text.text: More evidence built on researcher-defined outcomes may continue to reinforce those outcomes, leaving dimensions of value identified by children and teachers less visible.
This review also examined whether stakeholder participation continued across the conceptual, operational, and endorsed dimensions of educational value.
Stakeholders who helped define priorities during design were rarely reported as retaining similarly influential roles during evaluation (Section 4.5).
This discontinuity of social participation compounds the concern about what educational value the evidence ultimately reflects.

Stakeholders may help define priorities during design but play no part in deciding how the resulting value is endorsed, leaving little opportunity to check whether their priorities carry through to evaluation.
As a result, the evidence used to establish educational value may disproportionately reflect researcher-defined priorities.
Importantly, this does not mean that stakeholder participation must be identical at every stage.
Rather, it suggests that stakeholder-defined priorities can be lost as technologies move from design to measurement and evaluation.

This is particularly problematic given the heterogeneity of neurodivergent learners, who may experience and value different aspects of a technology, as may the teachers, schools, and families who support them (Sheejamol et al., 2025).

text.text: Drawing the findings together from Section 5.1, the evidence of educational value of neuroinclusive EdTech reflects a narrow set of outcomes and voices.

Conceptually, educational value was oriented towards individual, academic benefit: technologies were typically designed to adapt content or task demands to individual learners rather than to the classroom as a whole.
Operationally, this value was measured mainly through academic, cognitive, behavioural, or perceptual outcomes.
Finally, it was endorsed largely by researchers, with children and teachers rarely shaping what counted as success.

Here, conceptualisation refers to what counts as valuable, operationalisation to how value is translated into outcomes and measures, and endorsement to whose judgements determine whether value has been achieved.
These dimensions are analytically distinct but interconnected and shape which forms of educational value becomes visible in the evidence.

Research focuses disproportionately on autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual or cognitive disabilities, possibly reflecting historical research priorities and the prominence of these diagnostic categories in educational research.
Their association with particular educational purposes raises the possibility that diagnoses, rather than needs that cut across diagnostic categories, shape how educational needs are conceptualised.
This should be understood as a possibility suggested by the observed pattern rather than an established causal explanation.

Future research should broaden representation, particularly of underrepresented profiles such as developmental language disorder and co-occurring conditions, and examine whether links between diagnoses and educational purposes reflect children's needs or prevailing assumptions.
Needs-based approaches that prioritise children's experiences and support needs over diagnostic labels offer one way forward (Kapp et al., 2013; Pritchard-Rowe & Gibson, 2024).

text.text: Neuro-inclusive EdTech appears to be shaped primarily by researcher-led design and the affordances of emerging technologies, with limited evidence of development driven by needs identified by children and teachers.
Research concentrates around VR, robotics, and AI, with multimodality, feedback, and personalisation among the most common design principles.
This raises the question of whether design responds to identified educational needs or is also driven by technology research trends, particularly given the rarity of children as design partners.
This is particularly consequential for neurodivergent children, who may experience the same technology differently depending on their sensory, attentional, communicative, and cognitive needs.

Future research should prioritise participatory approaches that enable children and other stakeholders with diverse communication and participation profiles to shape both technology design and how educational value is defined (Iversen et al., 2017; Nowack et al., 2026).

text.text: The individualised orientation persists in classroom use and may position neuro-inclusion primarily as individual accommodation rather than classroom-level inclusion.
Individual accommodation asks how technology can help a learner engage with an existing task.
Classroom inclusion asks how technology reshapes classroom environment and practice to support diverse participation (Bauminger-Zviely et al., 2013; Fage et al., 2019).

text.text: These two approaches are not mutually exclusive and neuro-inclusive EdTech may require both individual responsiveness and classroom responsiveness (Göransson & Nilholm, 2014).

text.text: Future research should examine the relational consequences of individualised technology use within classroom dynamics, as well as small-group and whole-class models.
Longitudinal studies in authentic classrooms would be particularly valuable to help bridge the gap between EdTech advancements and practical implementation in schools.
A key gap concerns the construction of educational value.
Operational value often diverged from conceptual, and stakeholder influence was not consistently sustained across the conceptual, operational, and endorsed dimensions.
Participation appeared to function as a discrete step rather than a sustained process through which stakeholders iteratively shape how a technology's value is defined, measured, and endorsed.
The selection of outcomes, measures, and evaluators is consequential, as it shapes which forms of success become visible in the evidence and which forms of educational value remain unmeasured.
At a minimum, future research should align operational value with the conceptual.
Studies should report explicitly how each intended goal was operationalised and measured, and justify any new outcomes introduced at evaluation.
Beyond alignment, the field needs methods for situating these measures within stakeholders' priorities.
Stakeholders hold different interests, goals, and definitions of value, which shape which outcomes are prioritised and which strategies are adopted.
Building on this finding, one possible methodological direction is to adapt social multi-criteria evaluation for neuro-inclusive EdTech (Kucirkova et al., 2026; Livingstone & Pothong, 2025).
text.formatted: Building on this finding, one possible methodological direction is to adapt social multi-criteria evaluation for neuro-inclusive EdTech <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Kucirkova et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Livingstone & Pothong, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Criteria developed with relevant stakeholders, children, families, teachers, and researchers, could complement technical with social and educational perspectives, so that measured performance aligns with experienced value.
Standardised academic and behavioural measures remain valuable, but they should be complemented by, rather than replaced with, outcomes defined by learners and educators.
Advancing the field requires moving beyond whether an EdTech is effective to how its educational value is conceptually and operationally defined, for which contexts, and under whose authority.
Our first framework structures this shift across three levels (Figure 17).
text.formatted: Our first framework structures this shift across three levels <ref type="bibr">(Figure 17)</ref>.

text.text: At the conceptual level: future research should define neuro-inclusive EdTech for primary classrooms together with multiple stakeholders through participatory methods.
It should bridge the divide between individual accommodation and collective inclusion and address cross-cutting learner needs beyond narrow diagnostic labels.
At the operational level: researchers should ensure that operational value of educational success align with the conceptual, so that value measured in classrooms reflects intended value.

At the endorsement level: children, teachers, and families should participate in and influence evaluation, so that endorsed educational value reflects the priorities of those affected by the technology.

Stakeholder participation should also be continuous across all three levels, because priorities articulated during design can be reinterpreted, narrowed, or lost when researchers alone translate them into measures and judge whether they have been met.

Alongside such participatory approaches, broader evaluation infrastructure, such as common reporting standards and open repositories of outcome measures, would improve the transparency and comparability of evidence across studies.
This would strengthen its usefulness for decisionmaking by schools, procurement teams, and policymakers.
This review makes three main contributions to the literature on neuro-inclusive EdTech.

First, rather than focusing on a single technology, diagnostic population, or educational outcome, it integrates learner profiles, design processes, classroom adoption, and evaluation within a single analytic framework for primary school classrooms, revealing patterns across the technology lifecycle that remain invisible in narrower reviews.
Second, it proposes two complementary frameworks.

The research framework (Section 5.2.5) conceptualises educational value in terms of its conceptualisation, operationalisation, and endorsement dimensions, demonstrates that these can diverge, and introduces stakeholder continuity as a dimension of analysis.
The practitioner framework (Section 6) translates these dimensions into criteria for appraising technologies in practice.

Third, the review extends existing concerns about limited empirical evidence in this field (Lai et al., 2022; Lai & Bower, 2019; Ronksley-Pavia et al., 2025) by identifying a potential epistemic gap: increasing the volume of evidence alone may not resolve whose perspectives and definitions of educational value that evidence represents.

text.text: The contribution is therefore not simply to show that more research is needed, but that what counts as meaningful educational value in neuro-inclusive primary classrooms depends on what evidence is produced and whose priorities define and evaluate it.

We now turn to the implications of this framing of the educational value of neuro-inclusive EdTech for practice, in particular how it can help bridge the substantial gap between rapid advances in EdTech and its adoption in primary school classrooms (Kanders et al., 2024; Kucirkova et al., 2026).

This review provides a broad map of the neuro-inclusive EdTech literature for primary school classrooms across learner profiles, technologies, design processes, classroom adoption, and evaluation (see Section 5.3 for its principal contributions).
Despite these contributions, as with any study, this review also has limitations.
It was restricted to English-language studies from six databases, which may have excluded relevant work published elsewhere or in other languages.
Restricting inclusion to peer-reviewed publications excluded grey literature, such as white papers and reports.
The themes of interest were also broadly specified.
This was deliberate, as one of our primary aims was to map the landscape of EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary school classrooms, which is the purpose of a scoping review.
Future research could consider systematic reviews and, where sufficient methodological and outcome homogeneity exists, meta-analysis of specific technologyoutcome relationships.
This scoping review of 93 studies published between 2015 and 2026 reveals a narrow and fragmented understanding of educational value in EdTech for neuro-inclusive primary classrooms.

Existing research focuses predominantly on autistic learners and individualised academic and cognitive support, while social, communicative, peer-interaction and teachersupport outcomes receive less attention.

Design and evaluation processes remain largely researcher-led, the intended goals do not always align with those evaluated, and children's and educators' participation rarely extends from design to evaluation.
Educational value thus depends not only on which outcomes are prioritised, but also on how success is evaluated and whose perspectives inform these judgements.

To address these challenges, we propose two complementary conceptual frameworks: one to guide future research and development, and another to help practitioners assess the relevance and readiness of EdTech for specific classroom contexts.

Together, the frameworks connect the development and evaluation of EdTech with the practical judgements required for their use in classrooms, and provide a basis for integrating children's and educators' perspectives more systematically.

The contribution of this review thus extends beyond mapping the evidence on whether EdTech works by broadening the question to include what counts as educational value, how it is established, and for whom, offering a basis for more participatory, contextually grounded and educationally meaningful approaches to designing, adopting and evaluating EdTech for neuro-inclusive classrooms.
